source.title: Gradient Descent on Logistic Regression with Non-Separable Data and Large Step Sizes
source.authors: S. Meng; Antonio Orvieto; Dan Cao; Christopher De Sa

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including appendices; no apparent cutoff or garbling that prevents reading.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies large-step gradient-descent dynamics in non-separable logistic regression, an adjacent setting to the claim about neural-network training. Its own results do not test any listed version's neural-network behavior.
record.gate_note: The paper's experiments and proofs concern logistic regression. Neural-network findings in the text are cited prior work, not results of this study. Rows below capture the paper's own logistic-regression cycle results as related findings, not tests of the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The study proves and illustrates large-step GD dynamics in non-separable logistic regression. These results concern linear classifiers with logistic-like losses, not the neural networks specified in V1–V6. Its explicit comparison with edge-of-stability behavior does not test V5 in the systems that version names.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. Here λ is the largest Hessian eigenvalue at the minimizer. In one dimension, 0 < η ≤ 1/λ guarantees global convergence; for every 1 < γ ≤ 2, some dataset admits a stable cycle at η = γ/λ. Higher-dimensional counterexamples exist for every 0 < γ ≤ 2. These are existence results, not claims that every dataset cycles; the standard global guarantee for η < 2/L remains intact.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies constant-step gradient descent on non-separable logistic regression objectives, with theoretical constructions and numerical illustrations; it does not use the neural-network training recipes in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Cycle behavior depends on dataset construction, step size, dimension, and initialization. The paper notes that the real datasets used for Figure 1 showed no clear cycles below η = 2/λ, while constructed datasets produced cycles below that threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: Constructed non-separable logistic-regression datasets admit stable cycles below the minimizer's local stability threshold. Theorems establish examples for every 1 < γ ≤ 2 in one dimension and every 0 < γ ≤ 2 in higher dimensions, where η = γ/λ.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For non-separable logistic regression, local stability of the minimizer does not guarantee global convergence; dataset construction and initialization can instead lead GD to stable cycles.

fits_no_version.finding: One constructed one-dimensional example suggests chaos at γ = 1.5, but the authors do not establish it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Non-separable logistic regression may exhibit chaotic GD dynamics below the minimizer's local stability threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: Stacked logistic-regression constructions have sharpness settling above 2/η while loss stops decreasing and iterates continue cycling.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sharpness above 2/η need not produce self-stabilization and continued loss reduction in logistic regression without progressive sharpening.

record.problems: The principal cycle results are theoretical constructions with numerical illustrations, not broad empirical tests on standard benchmarks. For the Figure 1 real datasets, the authors report no clear cycles before η = 2/λ. The two-dimensional basin is numerical, and one Figure 5 case is described only as possibly chaotic.
record.rows_left_out: The bifurcation diagrams on the two LIBSVM datasets and the toy dataset report outcomes as figures without textual numerical values assignable to individual runs; omitted as separate rows. Figure 8 likewise gives figure-only dynamics without recoverable text values. Cited neural-network results are excluded because they are prior work, not this study's results.

record.verdict_notes: The record's T3 assignment should be T6 because none of the listed versions is tested. Row states are assessed against those versions; cannot_determine does not dispute the reported logistic-regression cycles. No missing result bears on V1–V6.
